Choosing courses

Sophia, Study.com, or StraighterLine: which courses should you take first?

Choose the degree requirements before choosing the subscription. Sophia, Study.com, and StraighterLine can serve different parts of a plan. The useful starting provider is the one whose available courses fill your remaining requirements at a cost and pace that work for you.

DegreeSteps editorial team6 min readReviewed 2026-11-27

Begin with the gaps in your degree plan

A provider can have a large catalog and a low monthly price without offering the particular course you need. Start with the receiving university, exact degree and format, and the requirements left after existing learning. Then compare the eligible course options for those rows.

This is especially important when several providers cover introductory subjects. If writing is already satisfied, another writing course may contribute nothing to the degree. If a course is accepted only as an elective and your elective space is full, the low purchase price does not make it a useful next step.

A provider’s ACE or NCCRS recommendation is part of its credit basis. It is separate from the receiving school’s decision to award credit and apply it to the degree. Keep the exact course identity, relevant recommendation dates, and receiving placement connected as you compare.

Compare the actual products being sold

Sophia’s current official pages agree on $99 for one month and $299 for four months before applicable tax, but its annual price is inconsistent: the pricing page advertises $799 and the account-and-billing tutorial lists $599. Confirm checkout before buying the annual product. These memberships automatically renew under their terms. Sophia ordinarily allows two active courses at a time; written or project-based Touchstones can add grading time. Compare the access you will use rather than assuming the longest purchase is cheapest for your basket.

Study.com’s current College Saver is listed at $95 per month, while College Saver Pro is $235. Course inclusion differs: Pro adds premium and upper-division options. The current plans advertise unlimited monthly completions with different concurrent-course limits. A study-help or test-preparation subscription is not the same as a credit-earning plan.

StraighterLine’s current profile lists a $99 monthly membership plus individual course charges. It also advertises selected-course packages with separate terms. Laboratory kits can add expense. Those structures should be compared with the exact courses in your basket rather than treated as one universal per-course rate.

Assessment style can change the right choice

Study.com’s August 25, 2026 support policy describes College Saver and Pro finals as open-book and non-proctored, with no separate final-exam charges. It permits up to three attempts with a three-day wait. Course assignments and identity verification still apply; the latter can use TypingDNA or a Veriff ID-and-selfie check. Older discussions about a different exam model may not describe the product currently offered.

StraighterLine’s current final Benchmark requirements use Honorlock, with a computer, Chrome extension, webcam identity check, and government ID. The exams remain open-book using authorized materials. Sophia’s official guidance describes open-book, non-proctored exams alongside Challenges, Milestones and course-specific written or project work.

Look at the actual course and assessment requirements when a testing format matters to you. A self-paced course can still include monitored exams, essays, projects, laboratories, or grading delays. Selecting a provider with a comfortable format can be more useful than picking the lowest headline price.

Make the course basket before the calendar

Choose a group of courses that fill genuine open requirements. Identify prerequisites, projects, laboratory materials, and expected feedback steps. Then decide how many you can realistically work on during the paid period, using your available study time rather than someone else’s completion story.

A hypothetical $99 monthly subscription spread across three applicable courses in one paid month is $33 per course before tax or other charges. If the same three courses take two paid months, the membership share is $66 per course. These are arithmetic scenarios, not a claim that three courses can be completed in a particular period.

The most expensive result is often a paid course that does not help the target degree. Time spent selecting the right basket can prevent that result. It can also reveal when you should delay a subscription until prerequisites, materials, or a university evaluation are ready.

One degree can use more than one provider

Our reviewed WGU Business Management starting proposal uses both Sophia and Study.com options to assign 69 of its 110 competency units outside WGU. That example does not establish a universal provider order for every student. It shows why the destination-specific course map matters.

Another student may have college courses that replace many of those introductory requirements. A student whose destination accepts institutional coursework but little alternative credit may need a different source entirely. The plan should adapt to those facts rather than force every learner into the same brand sequence.

When comparing options, keep the receiving award separate from the source credit quantity. A WGU requirement worth four competency units can be met by a published source course whose original credit amount is different. Do not multiply a provider’s price by an assumed universal conversion.

Pick the first purchase with a clear purpose

Before paying, identify the requirement each selected course fills, confirm the product includes it, and decide when you can give the course attention. Read the current assessment and cancellation terms for that product. Keep the receipt and original course record with the rest of your learning information.

You can begin by browsing the course library without choosing a university immediately. Save courses that interest you, then compare their supported degree placements before starting them. If you already know your degree, use its mapped requirements to choose a smaller, more useful basket.

About this research

DegreeSteps editorial team · Degree planning and transfer-credit research

We explain educational choices using university catalogs, receiving-school course agreements, provider guidance, and the same researched degree models used by DegreeSteps. Our articles distinguish proposed coursework, original learning records, and individual university awards. Worked examples identify their program, format, units, and relevant dates. Founder stories are attributed as reported experience, without invented transcripts, savings totals, or reviewer credentials.
